title: Note (Expenses): J T Forsyth Greenpark Garage Limited v Angus Council
text:
Lands Tribunal for Scotland

NOTE (Expenses)

J T Forsyth Greenpark Garage Limited (Applicant) v Angus Council (Respondent)

Introduction

[1] This case involves a claim for compensation on the basis of extinguishment of a business following upon the compulsory acquisition of a building. On the second day of the substantive hearing, 29 November 2022, following the conclusion of the applicant’s first witness, and the making of a query by the Tribunal, the applicant sought leave to withdraw from the proceedings under rule 22.

[2] We consented to the withdrawal, subject to the making of an award of expenses in favour of the respondent. We held a hearing on expenses on 7 December 2022. The applicant accepts that an order for expenses should be made, but the respondent seeks an award on the agent and client, third party paying, scale. The respondent also seeks expenses to be awarded on the Court of Session scale, and for sanction for the employment of counsel. The respondent further seeks certification for the employment of expert witnesses, namely Mr Greig Rowand CA and Mr Gerry McCluskey MRICS . The applicant does not oppose sanction for Mr Rowand but does oppose sanction for Mr McCluskey. Sanction for counsel is not opposed. The applicant submitted that expenses should be awarded on the sheriff court scale.

Respondent’s submissions

[3] Expenses should be on the Court of Session scale. The complexity of the case was acknowledged by the concession that it was reasonable for counsel to have been instructed. The case had many complex issues. The claim initially stood at over £1m and was subsequently reduced to a sum just over £765,000. The amount of compensation sought greatly exceeded the threshold for a Court of Session action, namely the sum of £100,000.

[4] Mr McCluskey had prepared a valuation report for the subjects compulsorily acquired, where compensation was payable to a third party landowner. He had provided a statement, amongst other things making reference to a proposed alternative site. It was also necessary for the applicant to obtain Mr McCluskey’s advice following the late addition of Mr Thornton- Kemsley to the applicant’s witness list on 22 November 2022, to deal with sections in the latter’s report, particularly relating to alternative sites.

[5] Turning to the issue of the agent/client scale, counsel referred to McKie v Scottish Ministers 2006 SC 528, Lord Hodge at para 3:-

“But, thirdly, where one of the parties has conducted their litigation incompetently or unreasonably, and thereby caused the other party unnecessary expense, the court can impose, as a sanction against such conduct, an award of expenses on the solicitor and client scale. Fourthly, in its consideration of the reasonableness of a party’s conduct of an action, the court can take into account all relevant circumstances. Those circumstances include the party’s behaviour before the action commenced, the adequacy of a party’s preparation for the action, the strengths or otherwise of a party’s position on the substantive merits of the action, the use of a court action for an improper purpose, and the way in which a party has used the court procedure, for example, to progress or delay the resolution of the dispute …”

[6] It was submitted that the applicant’s conduct had been incompetent and unreasonable, its preparation inadequate and its application had no merit at all. It was submitted that the claim was untrue from the beginning of the proceedings. The claim had been for extinguishment of business, in the sense understood in Prestwick Hotels Ltd v Glasgow Corp 1975 SC 105 at pp108-109, i.e. that no element of the old goodwill had survived. However, it was the case that on 22 March 2018, the applicant had executed a contract allowing another company, namely GPG Montrose Limited (“GPG”) to benefit from the goodwill of the applicant’s business carried out from the property at which it had until then traded. The conduct fell short of fraudulent, only since the respondent was aware that the claim was untrue. The applicant had produced a document stating that staff were transferred under TUPE to GPG and had thus intimated that its business retained its identity, and had been transferred to a third party.

[7] Counsel also accepted that the applicant had lodged a letter dated 21 January 2019 by its accountants, Murray Taylor (Scotland) Limited, apparently conceding that GPG may have acquired a customer base from the applicant, although stating in effect that in the circumstances any remaining customer base was irrelevant to the value of the goodwill. Nevertheless, the claim itself contradicted the fact that goodwill had been transferred to GPG. It was also the case that when the accounting experts met, they had not discussed the GPG issue because the applicant’s expert Mr Bell had been instructed not to discuss the GPG business; i.e. the fact that GPG had succeeded to the applicant’s goodwill.

[8] It was submitted that the applicant should have obtained and disclosed an expert report and its basis early in the proceedings, under reference to Cooper v Merck Sharp & Dohme Ltd [2012] CSOH 48 per Lord Brailsford at para 13. The report by Mr Thornton-Kemsley had exceeded the remit of an expert surveyor in addressing accounting issues for extinction of business. The Murray Taylor valuation lacked depth and reasoning.

[9] The issue of business extinction was placed in issue by the respondent’s answers, and ultimately on 15 August 2018, the Tribunal ordered the furnishing of further particulars by the applicant on the matter within 14 days. The applicant failed to do so and breached the order. This led to a motion for dismissal on 31 January 2019, in which the applicant indicated that it needed time to obtain an expert report and to adjust further. After further apparent inaction by the applicant, the respondent applied again for dismissal on 9 April 2019. The applicant sought more time to instruct an expert, and on 2 May 2019 the Tribunal Clerk indicated:

“The Tribunal wish to be clear that communication in general, from the applicant, must improve. Simply not responding to a deadline, particularly an extended one, and allowing it to pass with no update, is not good practice”.

[10] There was deadline of 30 May 2019 for further adjustments, which were not intimated and nor was an expert report produced or any explanation given for their absence. A report dated 22 May 2019 was finally lodged and intimated only on 29 August 2019. In effect the respondent had been required to pursue the absence of an expert report for a whole year from August 2018 to August 2019, being met with silence, breaches of Tribunal orders, and in one case an untrue statement from the applicant’s agent stating that the report had been lodged on 23 May when it had not been so lodged.

[11] Moreover, the applicant had not voluntarily disclosed the background accounting information to the respondent’s accounting expert which had been provided to the applicant’s expert. The Tribunal had indicated that this should be done at a hearing on 31 January 2019. Ultimately the Tribunal had to make an order for such documents on 9 September 2019. But nearly three years later, on 18 July 2022, the respondent still required a further order of the Tribunal for comprehensive disclosure of that information in terms of clauses 4, 7, 9 and 14 of a specification of documents. The applicant ought to have been able to provide the information promptly to the respondent by being in possession of a supporting expert report in 2018.

[12] Finally it was submitted that the applicant had simply never prepared to prove its claim and thus put the respondent and Tribunal to needless preparation work. For example, Appendix H of Mr Bell’s accountancy report asserted 11 heads of loss for compensation in the sum of £31,683, but no primary evidence was produced for any of these matters or indeed any evidence at all. All the kinds of loss would in ordinary course be recorded in writing such as by invoices, receipts, reports etc., but these had not been produced. This evidenced both incompetence and unreasonable conduct of litigation.

[13] Similarly, the applicant’s main witness Mr Forsyth referred to a variety of documents in his witness statement, none of which were produced. Written advice from accountants that the applicant should cease trading, on the basis of having lost an important contract, was not vouched. Contemporary financial records made in the course of carrying out the business, including financial statements, were not produced apart from a number of P60 certificates. Much of the material which was available to the Tribunal had in fact been lodged by the respondent who had incurred expense in seeking to assist the Tribunal. The late production of witness statements were all of a piece in the lack of preparation by the applicant.

[14] We referred counsel to Aberdeen District Council v Emslie & Simpson Ltd 1995 SCLR 317 IH whereby Lord Morison, with whose opinion the others agreed, indicated that it was reasonable in a compulsory purchase case that:-

“… a claimant should put forward his claim on the maximum basis which he can reasonably support and should be entitled to the expenses of doing so if he is successful in the general assertion of his right.”

[15] Counsel submitted that emphasis was put on the word “reasonably”, it could not be right that a claimant should put forward a claim which could not be reasonably supported, as was the case here.

Applicant’s submissions

[16] Mr McCluskey should not be sanctioned as an expert witness. He was partly a witness to fact to speak to his negotiations on behalf of the council. His valuation report was not relevant to the issue between the present parties. His witness statement contained nothing about his views on the suitability of alternative sites; it would appear that the respondent had another witness Mr Wilson, the CPO project manager, available to do so. Mr McCluskey’s statement did not aim to provide independent assistance on matters within his expertise.

[17] Just because the claim exceeded £100,000, it did not mean that the Court of Session scale was appropriate. Complex cases could be heard in the sheriff court.

[18] Reference was made to three of the cases cited in McKie v Scottish Ministers ; namely British Railways Board v Ross & Cromarty Council 1974 SC 27, Walker v MacNeill 1981 SLT (N) 21 and Baker Hughes v CGC Contracting International 2005 1 SC 65. These cases had a common theme, namely, that the matter in question ought not to have been the subject of litigation. The current application was different; the applicant required to be compensated for the fact that the warehouse it occupied had been the subject of a CPO. The applicant had acted on advice, namely, advice from its accountant that the business could not survive the loss of the warehouse, and that a disturbance claim for loss of profit that might enable the business to survive was uncertain in its prospects, as appeared from a report by Mr Thornton-Kemsley.

[19] It was recognised that the claim for business extinguishment might have been difficult in the absence of a fall-back position, but this did not make the claim false. The respondent’s submission emphasised its analysis of the case, which was different from the applicant’s analysis. What was in dispute was the decision of the applicant at the time to close its business on account of the loss of the police contract. It may have placed its eggs in one basket by claiming for extinction, where some goodwill had been retained, but the existing customer base could not be guaranteed to make a profit. The case had not been conducted in the sort of extraordinary fashion displayed in the three cases cited. An award of expenses was sufficient acknowledgement for the failure of the claim. The case was also quite different to the case of Cooper v Merck Sharp & Dohme Ltd.

[20] Issues surrounding the timing of instructing, producing and supplying documents relating to the expert report were managed by the Tribunal at the time. The burden of expenses in such matters was not a question to be rolled into the issue of reasonableness of the proceedings as a whole. There had been very extensive recoveries by way of specification and the sharing of all materials seen by the applicant’s agent. The applicant’s agent had wished to focus on issues remaining in dispute between the parties. It was accepted that the respondent’s productions had evidential value to both parties, so an award of expenses on the ordinary basis would be sufficient to recognise the respondent’s contribution in this regard.

Discussion

[21] In the first place we are satisfied that the case was of sufficient complexity and potential value to merit the employment of counsel, and for expenses to be taxed on the Court of Session scale.

[22] Secondly, we think it appropriate for Mr McCluskey to be certified as an expert, as well as Mr Rowand. It is true that Mr McCluskey’s witness statement did not really deal with the live issue of alternative sites. However, given the late involvement, or perhaps more precisely the renewed involvement of Mr Thornton-Kemsley MRICS , whereby he was added to the applicant’s list of witnesses in the week before the hearing, we think it was necessary to have Mr McCluskey on standby as a witness. He would have been able to speak to the comparative condition of the subjects and at least one of the alternative sites, which was put in issue by Mr Forsyth’s evidence. Mr McCluskey would also have been able to discuss the alternative sites more generally, from the perspective of a surveyor, in response to the evidence by Mr Thornton-Kemsley. So we think it was reasonable to employ him as an expert witness.

[23] Thirdly, in determining whether to allow expenses on the agent/client scale, we think Lord Hodge’s summary in McKie v Scottish Ministers is apt for compulsory purchase compensation cases. We see no tension between an analysis of the reasonableness of a party’s conduct in an action in the context of an award of expenses on the agent/client scale, and the making of a claim on the maximum basis which can be reasonably supported in the sense used by the Inner House in Aberdeen District Council v Emslie & Simpson Ltd . In both cases, the court may look at all the facts and circumstances as to whether or not a claimant has acted reasonably.

[24] We also bear in mind the opinion of Lady Smith in Baker Hughes v CGC Contracting International where she said at para. 18:-

“I noted from the Scottish authorities referred to that expenses had been awarded on a higher scale in cases where the Court was satisfied that the circumstances were ‘exceptional’ … that a party’s conduct was ‘unreasonable’ … that it was ‘less than reasonable’ … and that it showed ‘a substantial degree of irresponsibility’ … Clearly, there are cases where the Court has exercised its discretion to award expenses on the higher scale as a means of marking its disapproval of the conduct of one party to the litigation.”

[25] A serious concern as to the conduct of the present litigation relates to the transfer for value of the goodwill of the applicant’s business to the new company GPG. This was, of course, known to the applicant and is evidenced by the agreement of 22 March 2018. The question of retention of goodwill was keenly focussed upon by the respondent to the extent of obtaining an order for further particulars, under threat of dismissal. Yet the claim as adjusted states:

“The company did not transfer the garage business to GPG. GPG runs a separate and smaller business that occupies only a part of the former premises of the company … a reasonable person in business would be entitled to take the view that for the applicant to seek to reconfigure their business along similar lines would be too risky a proposition.”

[26] An implication from the above appears to be that the goodwill was not transferred to the new business. Another implication is, perhaps, that any goodwill transferred to the new company was not useful. But in any event the claim proceeds to seek compensation for the loss of the whole of the applicant’s goodwill on the basis that the business was extinguished. It is no doubt true that the applicant’s position was based upon the Murray Taylor letter of 21 January 2019, which had been disclosed, and which argued, in effect, that the value of the goodwill was irrelevant. It concedes that “GPG may have acquired a customer base.” But it seems to us that the undisputed fact there was a retention of goodwill was an inherent contradiction to the applicant’s position in the proceedings: i.e. that the applicant should be compensated for the whole value of its goodwill.

[27] In these circumstances the applicant’s written evidence appeared to ignore an elephant in the room, namely that the goodwill had been let or assigned for value to GPG. The applicant did not attempt to set out any fall-back position in the pleadings or the written evidence which might have valued a partial loss of goodwill. We feel that this degree of hubris has resulted in predictable consequences.

[28] Additionally, we are driven to the conclusion that the case has been exceptionally poorly prepared. We give only the most egregious examples. After considerable delay in obtaining an expert report and anticipated adjustments, in the light of a failure to furnish further particulars within a deadline, the applicant’s agent’s failure to communicate while a deadline was allowed to pass earned a rebuke from the Tribunal’s Clerk on 2 May 2019. We shall give the applicant the benefit of the doubt and not pass adverse comment in respect of the need for a drawn out and tortuous procedure for the recovery of documents involving two orders for commission and diligence (15 August 2018 and 18 July 2022) and one order for express production (9 September 2019). However, the inability of the applicant to produce any hearing documents in the form of vouchers for costs incurred due to the CPO in the sum of £31,683 is inexplicable. Furthermore, the applicant’s witness statements (apart from reports) ought to have been produced by 31 October 2022 under the timetable, but the respondent was forced to make a motion on 21 November 2022 to compel the witness statements to be produced in the week before the hearing, as they were on 23 November 2022, i.e. over three weeks beyond the deadline. Complex litigation cannot be run in such a haphazard manner.

[29] Perhaps none of the above, on its own, would amount to unreasonable prosecution of the litigation. However, in combination, we regret that we are forced to conclude that for those at the receiving end of the applicant’s conduct, the conduct has been unreasonable. Accordingly we shall award expenses on the agent/client, third party paying basis.

Conclusion

[30] We shall consent to the applicant withdrawing from the proceedings under rule 22. We find the applicant liable to the respondent in the expenses of the proceedings, as taxed on the Court of Session scale and on an agent/client, third party paying basis. We shall sanction the employment of counsel. We shall certify Mr Rowand and Mr McCluskey as expert witnesses for the respondent, with reference to our comments on the remit of Mr McCluskey as discussed in para. 22 above.

Members sitting: R A Smith, QC ; A Oswald, FRICS
Decision issued: 18 May 2023
Case Ref: LTS/COMP/2018/0001

Certified a true copy of the statement of reasons for the decision of the Lands Tribunal for Scotland intimated to parties on 18 May 2023
